Caterpiller
KAT-er-pil-er
noun
The KJV’s spelling of caterpillar, from the Old French chatepelose, “hairy cat,” from the shagginess of the creature; hence the devouring larva. In Joel it renders the Hebrew chasil, from a root meaning “to consume, to finish off.”

Biblical Definition

Caterpiller is the KJV’s spelling of caterpillar, and in Joel it is the last of the four devourers, rendering the Hebrew chasil, from a root meaning to consume or to finish off. It comes at the end of the roll: “that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten” (Joe 1:4) — the finisher, that takes the last leaf the others spared. In the psalm of Israel’s history the caterpiller is one of the plagues upon Egypt: “He gave also their increase unto the caterpiller, and their labour unto the locust” (Psa 78:46). Mark the word gave. Egypt’s increase did not fall to the worm by chance; God gave it. The whole labour of a mighty nation was handed over to a crawling thing, that Pharaoh might learn who reigns. Isaiah uses the creature for the plunder of Assyria’s host: “your spoil shall be gathered like the gathering of the caterpiller: as the running to and fro of locusts shall he run upon them” (Isa 33:4) — the spoiler is spoiled, and the plunder is stripped from him as swiftly as a swarm strips a field. So the caterpiller is God’s finishing servant, sent upon Egypt, upon Assyria, and upon a backslidden Israel alike. And to the last of the devourers the last of the promises is joined: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm” (Joe 2:25). What God gave to the worm, God can give back.

Webster 1828 Definition

The KJV’s spelling of caterpillar; the devouring larva that finishes what the other worms leave, rendering the Hebrew chasil.

CATERPILLER, the KJV spelling of caterpillar; the worm-like larva that devours leaves and herbage.

From the Old French chatepelose, “hairy cat,” from the shagginess of the creature.

It renders the Hebrew chasil, from a root “to consume, to finish off.”

It is the last of the four devourers in Joel’s rank (Joe 1:4).

God gave Egypt’s increase unto the caterpiller (Psa 78:46).

Key Scripture

Joe 1:4 — "That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten; and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten."

Psa 78:46 — "He gave also their increase unto the caterpiller, and their labour unto the locust."

Isa 33:4 — "And your spoil shall be gathered like the gathering of the caterpiller: as the running to and fro of locusts shall he run upon them."

Joe 2:25 — "And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but an old spelling for a devouring larva; it recovers that God gives the harvest to the worm and takes back what He gave.

expand to see more

The word rebukes the notion of a world that runs itself. “He gave also their increase unto the caterpiller” — the psalmist will not say that Egypt suffered a blight; he says God gave the increase away. The labour of a mighty kingdom was handed over to a crawling worm by the deliberate act of the LORD, and the plague was a sermon to Pharaoh on who governs the field. To read such a judgment as bad seasons and poor husbandry is to be blinder than Pharaoh, who at least knew that he was being struck and by whom.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the smallest creature and the largest empire. He set the caterpiller upon Egypt’s increase, and He ordered the spoiler’s spoil to be gathered like the gathering of the caterpiller, stripping Assyria as swiftly as a swarm strips a field. The same hand that gives to the worm restores the years the worm ate. Nothing is too small to be His servant and nothing too great to be His subject; and the God who commands the caterpiller commands the whole account of a man’s losses, and can give them back.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a devouring larva; it is the KJV’s spelling of caterpillar.

Caterpiller — the KJV’s spelling of caterpillar.

From Old French chatepelose, “hairy cat,” from the creature’s shagginess.

It renders the Hebrew chasil, “the consumer, the finisher.”

It is the last of Joel’s four devourers (Joe 1:4).

God gave Egypt’s increase and Assyria’s spoil to it (Psa 78:46; Isa 33:4).

Usage

"That which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten — the finisher takes the last leaf."

"He gave their increase unto the caterpiller: Egypt’s labour handed to a worm by God’s own act."

"The years the caterpiller ate the LORD promises to restore — He gave, and He gives back."
